Or are you suggesting that the consensus client just "suggests" the coinbase, and the execution client can then decide whether to use it or not? Ultimately the execution client can always override the coinbase if it wants but I think it's very useful for the consensus client to be able to send a coinbase it requests be used. What benefits does that provide other than making it easier to outsource execution client (something that we actively want to discourage)? What bugs me about this change is that it adds complexity and the only "positive" benefit I see is it allows people to do a thing we don't want them to do. Different validators on the same validator client may want to use a different coinbase. Could be someone running a validator for other family members, could be just not wanting to so publicly tie the two validators together. There's going to be plenty of user demand for this so it's getting implemented. The only real question is whether it's in the spec or not. In this case, I don't think we should cater to user demand, but instead to network security. The network is more secure against censorship attacks if every validator has its own execution client. I believe that we should be strongly "encouraging" that, or at least not actively adding complexity that makes it easier to not do that. Regardless of *why* you are having multiple consensus clients per execution client, IMO it is less healthy for the network than if you have one execution client per consensus client. The case of "family members" you mentioned is no different from outsourcing to infura, you are just outsourcing a bit more locally. 🙂 I think if we want one execution client per validator then we should focus on aligning incentives towards that (e.g proof of custody). Which is all the more reason we shouldn't add complexity to the protocol for a use case we are actively trying to design away. That's quite unhelpful really. We've had mining pools for ages and now we have staking pools. And the staking pools are entirely capable and incentivised to maintain a fork of clients that lets them run fewer execution engines as it's going to save them money. Hence, it's going to get implemented one way or the other. We don't *want* mining pools or staking pools though. You are suggesting that the core developers spend time/energy/resources building a feature so people can do a thing we don't want them to do. Sure, we cannot stop them from doing it, but we certainly can choose to not *help* them do the thing we don't want. I'm saying you're seriously over-inflating the value of not doing this and I suspect also overinflating the complexity of implementing it. It's a pretty simple thing. There is value in listening to what users want and not just saying we know better. 🙂 And as always, if we think security is an issue the way to solve it is by getting the incentives aligned not just hoping someone won't build the exploit. My calculus here is this: 1. The only benefit this change provides is to make it easier for people to pool. 2. We do not want people to pool. 3. This change requires non-zero work. Conclusion: We are doing non-zero work to make it easier for people to do a thing that we don't want people to do. excerpts.author: jgm
excerpts.content:
On the "every validator should run an execution client" thing: this is dangerously simplistic.  I can go for "we should maximize the number of execution clients", as that is a far more realistic goal.

To be clear: an execution client is a very heavyweight piece of code.  It takes up a lot of CPU, memory, network and disk resource.  As it is, many consensus clients use a centralized service because the requirements are too large for their home setups to handle.

Running anywhere near a 1:1 ratio for execution clients to validators is unrealistic for everyone.  We can argue as to _why_, but the reality of it is clear.  If coinbase was not available in the spec version of the API it would result in there having to be a non-compliant fork (no doubt only of geth and one or two of the "big three" consensus clients, reducing decentralization of choice and increasing operational risk).  It would  result in overall fewer public instances of execution clients, as fewer people would want to run and keep up-to-date with forked software.  It may well end up with a paid-for service, where ultimately most people go through the same gateway to fetch their execution blocks, reducing the number further.

Given that the choice for each staker, with whatever way they have decided to stake to date, is either to run an execution client or not the aim should be to find the ways to maximize the number of execution clients.  This is done by increasing the benefits compared to the costs.  The simple fact that there are a large number of stakers that run execution clients should be applauded, given that to date the benefits are near-0 and the costs a very significant part of the overall infrastructure.  Increasing costs, especially in such an obnoxious way as to cripple the functionality of a node for a purist view of how the world should be and contrary to everything that has been built to date, would be a most regrettable step.

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content:
I think their's an abuse of terms causing confusion here

A proof-of-custody on the execution layer would mix in a secret (e.g. privatekey) with the execution that can be trustlessly verified becoming a validity rule on the entire thing (eithr validity rule or later fraud proof on a reveal of a secret). This does not require a 1:1 relationship between *validators* and execution engines, but requires a validator to mix in a secret with whatever execution engine they run -- leading more naturally to a 1:1 ratio on **validator_client** and execution engine

The security model is similar to proof-of-custody for data. Either you did your own execution of that layer or you had to outsource a secret to a third party that could get your slashed

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: For something heavy like execution or data availability, there is distinctly a tragedy of the commons issue where it makes more sense to just follow the leader on voting on what the majority sees as correct

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: thus the integration of crypto ecnomic methods that proof you either did the work yourself or took on counter party risk to get slashed

excerpts.author: jgm
excerpts.content:
A balanced relationship between validator client and execution client makes more sense, although predicating a 1:1 relationship does make it a lot harder to build resilient infrastructure in a sane way (eg a pool of execution clients available to a set of execution clients on a per-request basis).

But even in a world where we have a simple 1:1 validator client and execution client it will be a requirement to be able to have different coinbases for the validators of each validator client.

excerpts.author: potuz
excerpts.content: And also notice that there's actually an impact on decentralization on how many you run. A simple thought exercise is this: if the whole network is 200K  validators and are held by one person. It's 100% centralized. If 1 of those validators are run by someone else it's still 100% centralized. If 100K on the other hand are run by a different person then it's only 50% "centralized"
